chunks.text: I'm Tucker Balch. We're here with Tamra Kamel, founder of Quandl. We're going to dive now into

chunks.title: Interview with Tammer Kamel (Part 1)
chunks.text: details about how the Quandl platform works. So let's start with sort of a big picture.

chunks.title: Interview with Tammer Kamel (Part 1)
chunks.text: Imagine I'm a hedge fund and I'm interested in working with Quandl. How does Quandl fit into my

chunks.title: Interview with Tammer Kamel (Part 1)
chunks.text: workflow? Right. So in any hedge fund where quantitative thinking is some or part of the

chunks.title: Interview with Tammer Kamel (Part 1)
chunks.text: investment strategy, then at the very start of that process is good high quality data.

chunks.title: Interview with Tammer Kamel (Part 1)
chunks.text: And that's where Quandl starts and finishes in a sense. We view it as our mission to get

chunks.title: Interview with Tammer Kamel (Part 1)
chunks.text: the data that professional investors need into their hands and into the format that they need

chunks.title: Interview with Tammer Kamel (Part 1)
chunks.text: it in. So Quandl offers a hedge fund literally dozens of mechanisms to pull that data, whether

chunks.title: Interview with Tammer Kamel (Part 1)
chunks.text: it's a low level API and they can pull the data right into a database that they're maintaining

chunks.title: Interview with Tammer Kamel (Part 1)
chunks.text: themselves or into Python or R or Matlab or Stata or any analysis tool they might be using.

chunks.title: Interview with Tammer Kamel (Part 1)
chunks.text: But we consider our job sort of mission accomplished for Quandl if we quickly and painlessly get

chunks.title: Interview with Tammer Kamel (Part 1)
chunks.text: the hedge fund, the data they need into the system they want.

chunks.title: Interview with Tammer Kamel (Part 1)
chunks.text: Now presumably this includes a combination of historical data and live data. Are all of your feeds historical

chunks.title: Interview with Tammer Kamel (Part 1)
chunks.text: as well as live or there's some that are special in some way?

chunks.title: Interview with Tammer Kamel (Part 1)
chunks.text: Right. So all of our data is historical for sure and updated daily. Live data is a little bit in the future for us.

chunks.title: Interview with Tammer Kamel (Part 1)
chunks.text: It's not available on the platform as of this moment.

chunks.title: Interview with Tammer Kamel (Part 1)
chunks.text: So I could imagine a flow something like this. Lots of people are on a daily cycle.

chunks.title: Interview with Tammer Kamel (Part 1)
chunks.text: You know, I think that's the majority of what people do. You might read historical data to inform

chunks.title: Interview with Tammer Kamel (Part 1)
chunks.text: your model or, you know, build some sort of model. But after market close you wait some period until

chunks.title: Interview with Tammer Kamel (Part 1)
chunks.text: the market day is available and then whatever data one might pull from Quandl. Do some number crunching

chunks.title: Interview with Tammer Kamel (Part 1)
chunks.text: overnight and then sort of put in orders for, you know, what you might do the next day. Now,

chunks.title: Interview with Tammer Kamel (Part 1)
chunks.text: what time does your data, what time is your data available and what mechanisms do people use to pull it?

chunks.title: Interview with Tammer Kamel (Part 1)
chunks.text: Yeah, so what you described is really a canonical use case for Quandl, right? A fund or an analyst

chunks.title: Interview with Tammer Kamel (Part 1)
chunks.text: will take the historical data, build and calibrate a model. And when they're comfortable that it's ready

chunks.title: Interview with Tammer Kamel (Part 1)
chunks.text: for action, then they're going to start executing on it. So Quandl market data is updated pretty quickly.

chunks.title: Interview with Tammer Kamel (Part 1)
chunks.text: after the close within minutes or depending on the, you know, the exact database we're talking about,

chunks.title: Interview with Tammer Kamel (Part 1)
chunks.text: hours. So, but definitely in time to run today's numbers through your model to get the output and

chunks.title: Interview with Tammer Kamel (Part 1)
chunks.text: know what actions need to be taken on the next trading day. So I love to learn details about how

chunks.title: Interview with Tammer Kamel (Part 1)
chunks.text: people build complex financial systems. So where do your machines live? So Quandl is quite modern in

chunks.title: Interview with Tammer Kamel (Part 1)
chunks.text: that respect. Everything lives in the cloud. We're a customer of Amazon's like so many others are. At the

chunks.title: Interview with Tammer Kamel (Part 1)
chunks.text: heart of Quandl is a modern NoSQL database and that's where the 15, 16 million time series, few billion data

chunks.title: Interview with Tammer Kamel (Part 1)
chunks.text: points live there. On top of that we've built an API and then the Quandl website itself, interestingly,

chunks.title: Interview with Tammer Kamel (Part 1)
chunks.text: is itself just another client of the Quandl API. If you were to look at our website you would discover

chunks.title: Interview with Tammer Kamel (Part 1)
chunks.text: it's perfectly orthodox. Nothing, it's a, it's a, it's a standard Ruby on Rails website built very

chunks.title: Interview with Tammer Kamel (Part 1)
chunks.text: conventionally and it's just another client of the Quandl API. Why the choice of NoSQL? So it, because,

chunks.title: Interview with Tammer Kamel (Part 1)
chunks.text: because of scalability, right, we want, we really need to be able to deliver lots of numerical data to

chunks.title: Interview with Tammer Kamel (Part 1)
chunks.text: lots of people very, very quickly and you know while we're still, you know, we're number of data points

chunks.title: Interview with Tammer Kamel (Part 1)
chunks.text: in the Quandl databases in the order of a few billion now, but we expect that to be at 10 or 20

chunks.title: Interview with Tammer Kamel (Part 1)
chunks.text: or 50 billion within a year or two and at that point conventional relational databases get kind of

chunks.title: Interview with Tammer Kamel (Part 1)
chunks.text: difficult to work with. So the, the glue between the various components is Ruby on Rails?

chunks.title: Interview with Tammer Kamel (Part 1)
chunks.text: It is indeed, yeah. So it's NoSQL and Ruby on Rails and that's it?

chunks.title: Interview with Tammer Kamel (Part 1)
chunks.text: That is it. It's, you know, Quandl is, you know, by software engineering standards, pretty plain vanilla

chunks.title: Interview with Tammer Kamel (Part 1)
chunks.text: simple implementation. Where, where Quandl, you know, where we sweat day-to-day is usually in maintaining

chunks.title: Interview with Tammer Kamel (Part 1)
chunks.text: the accuracy of 12 million data sets. The technical infrastructure is, you know, not to say it's trivial,

chunks.title: Interview with Tammer Kamel (Part 1)
chunks.text: but it's, it's conventional best practices software engineering.

chunks.title: Interview with Tammer Kamel (Part 1)
chunks.text: Getting back to the data, tell me a little bit about time stamping. Let me, let me tell you what I'm, what I'm getting at.

chunks.title: Interview with Tammer Kamel (Part 1)
chunks.text: So let's just consider market close data. So the price for a particular stock, you know, essentially is stamped at 4 o'clock.

chunks.title: Interview with Tammer Kamel (Part 1)
chunks.text: So one potential time stamp for that data is, you know, New York time. One potential time stamp for that data is 4 p.m.

chunks.title: Interview with Tammer Kamel (Part 1)
chunks.text: But maybe I can't observe it until 4 o'clock. That's just one example. But I'm curious, does that sort of time stamping feed into what you all do?

chunks.title: Interview with Tammer Kamel (Part 1)
chunks.text: Yeah, no, that's actually a really good point. And I suppose what you're getting at is the risk of creating a look-ahead bias in your analysis, right?

chunks.title: Interview with Tammer Kamel (Part 1)
chunks.text: Yeah, you know what? I can't claim that Quandl has any sort of panaceas for that sort of thing. We really, you know, we time stamp the data, of course, right?

chunks.title: Interview with Tammer Kamel (Part 1)
chunks.text: And, and the, the meticulous, diligent analyst should be aware of this kind of thing. And they'll see that, you know, the, the, this database is the 4 p.m. closing pressure.

chunks.title: Interview with Tammer Kamel (Part 1)
chunks.text: I think it's more likely to occur with things like earnings reports or something like that.

chunks.title: Interview with Tammer Kamel (Part 1)
chunks.text: Yeah. Well, with those sort of things, we're very, we are, you know, I mean, we reach to the vendors and the publishers for this, but they, they are acutely aware of that.

chunks.title: Interview with Tammer Kamel (Part 1)
chunks.text: So you'll see, take for example, our earnings data, there's both as reported sort of point in time data and revised data.

chunks.title: Interview with Tammer Kamel (Part 1)
chunks.text: So, you know, those kind of blatant risks of, of, of look-ahead bias, those are well mitigated.

chunks.title: Interview with Tammer Kamel (Part 1)
chunks.text: You know, when you look at your various vendors who are providing you data, what, what sorts of flaws do you see in that data?

chunks.title: Interview with Tammer Kamel (Part 1)
chunks.text: And what sorts of steps do you, do you have to take to mitigate those, those flaws?

chunks.title: Interview with Tammer Kamel (Part 1)
chunks.text: Yeah, it's interesting. The, the, you know, of course, there's no, there's no such thing as a perfect data set in this world, right?

chunks.title: Interview with Tammer Kamel (Part 1)
chunks.text: And we're, of course, strongly motivated to get as close to that ideal as possible.

chunks.title: Interview with Tammer Kamel (Part 1)
chunks.text: The way we've done it is kind of simple, but also a little bit original.

chunks.title: Interview with Tammer Kamel (Part 1)
chunks.text: And it falls from the mechanism we've set up where consumers of data have a direct relationship with the publishers of those data.

chunks.title: Interview with Tammer Kamel (Part 1)
chunks.text: And indeed the publisher of the data's livelihood depends on keeping that consumer satisfied and happy.

chunks.title: Interview with Tammer Kamel (Part 1)
chunks.text: And so unlike sort of many other data platforms where there's a lot of opacity between the end user and a lot of layers too,

chunks.title: Interview with Tammer Kamel (Part 1)
chunks.text: between the end user and the actual publisher. In fact, you might in many cases not even be able to reach the publisher.

chunks.title: Interview with Tammer Kamel (Part 1)
chunks.text: Quandl, there's this direct relation. So what you find is that if and when there's errors in the data,

chunks.title: Interview with Tammer Kamel (Part 1)
chunks.text: our publishers are very keen to correct it and fast because they've got five or ten or fifty customers who know it's them responsible for it.

chunks.title: Interview with Tammer Kamel (Part 1)
chunks.text: And they're keen to keep these people paying for the service, right?

chunks.title: Interview with Tammer Kamel (Part 1)
chunks.text: So it's, this is an amazing, you know, this is a reality that happens with many marketplaces.

chunks.title: Interview with Tammer Kamel (Part 1)
chunks.text: When you start removing the distance between the end consumer and the actual producer of the product, you get this quality improvement.

chunks.title: Interview with Tammer Kamel (Part 1)
chunks.text: The other thing that of course affects that is good old healthy competition on a marketplace, right?

chunks.title: Interview with Tammer Kamel (Part 1)
chunks.text: We actually right now for some, for some databases we have two or more vendors offering competing products.

chunks.title: Interview with Tammer Kamel (Part 1)
chunks.text: And nothing drives quality control like competition.

chunks.title: Interview with Tammer Kamel (Part 1)
chunks.text: Sure. Okay. Great interview. Thanks very much.

chunks.title: Interview with Tammer Kamel (Part 1)
chunks.text: I'm sure the students out there will find this fascinating. Thanks for your time. I really, really appreciate that.
